Subject: TTFT & Streaming SLO follow-up / Acme Health

Hi Samir / Nina —

Thanks again for taking the call earlier — good to align on the streaming use case and the latency targets you need for the new clinical assistant feature. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps: 

Recap (what we heard)
- Primary goal: streaming conversational responses in the clinician UI; UX requires first partial token to appear very quickly so clinicians see activity while the model continues streaming.
- TTFT target: <= 150ms median for short responses (<= 64 tokens); spike target <= 250ms for 95th percentile.
- Sustained throughput: 200 QPS across the fleet during clinic hours with concurrency up to 1,000 concurrent streams.
- Streaming transport: prefer SSE for browser-native integration; open to WebSocket if we need bi-directional. Chunk cadence desired: ~150–300ms between SSE chunks for perceived interactivity; minimum useful chunk size ~16–32 tokens.

Questions / clarifications we raised on the call
- Are requests typically short (<= 64 tokens) or do you expect long-form replies (> 256 tokens) in some flows? (you mentioned short prompts for quick clarifications, plus occasional long narratives)
- Do you plan on using client-side latency compensation (optimistic UI) or need guaranteed TTFT SLO for every token?

Attachments I’m including:
- [Attachment: acme-ttft-requirements.xlsx (Excel, 12KB)] (your detailed SLO spreadsheet)
- [Attachment: redwood-slo-matrix.pdf (PDF, 48KB)] (example SLO/rollback matrix we discussed)

Proposed next steps
1) Rishi to run a quick engineering feasibility pass + ask any clarifying technical questions (I’ve looped him in).
2) We’ll propose a short benchmark plan (3–4 day perf run) to surface realistic TTFT numbers on our Dedicated nodes & a small hosted pilot.
3) Align on transport (SSE vs WebSocket) and provide a minimal integration sample for your frontend team.

Can you confirm the TTFT targets above are accurate and share any additional peak concurrency windows (time ranges) we should provision for?

Thanks,

—Marissa Cole
Enterprise AE, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com

Subject: Re: TTFT & Streaming SLO follow-up / Acme Health

Thanks Marissa — that captures the convo well. Confirming:
- TTFT goal: median <=150ms for the short flows; 95p target <=250ms.
- Typical request size: ~40–80 tokens for tier-1 clinician queries; about 10% of requests may be longer (200–400 tokens) when pulling case summaries.
- Peak concurrency: weekdays 08:00–12:00 local (PST) we see the highest load; expect ~1,000 concurrent clinicians across regions, but initial pilot will be one region ~250 concurrent.

We prefer SSE for the browser integration to start; we may evaluate WebSocket later if we need client->server streaming. Chunk cadence of ~200ms sounds right — we’d rather smaller cadence than big bulk chunks.

Happy to run the pilot in the west region. Please send the benchmark plan and any firewall/AWS connectivity checklist.

—Samir
Director, Platform Engineering
Acme Health
samir@acmehealth.com

Hi Samir — quick technical follow-ups based on your notes: 

1) Workload mix: thanks for the token distribution — that helps a lot. For TTFT on short requests we typically optimize by:
   - Using small-batch / low-latency mode for head requests (dedicated lanes for TTFT-critical traffic).
   - Prefix caching where applicable to avoid re-computation for repeated prompts.

2) Transport: SSE is fine and generally simpler for one-way streaming. A few implementation notes:
   - We’ll stream server-sent events with chunk boundaries aligned to model-generated partials. Expect chunk cadence to be influenced by generation throughput; we can configure chunk flush to target ~150–250ms.
   - If you need deterministic chunk cadence <100ms we may need more aggressive batching tradeoffs and higher CPU/GPU overhead.

3) Benchmarks / telemetry: for the pilot we’ll collect: TTFT (median/95p), tokens-per-second throughput, concurrency scaling curve, and chunk latency distribution. Please confirm if you want us to also capture client observed latency (browser render time) via a small RUM snippet.

4) Network/connectivity: we’ll share a short connectivity checklist (IP allowlist, TLS cert expectations, optional VPC peering steps) in the next email.

Proposed benchmark plan (high level)
- Day 0: baseline perf on a sample workload with synthetic traffic matching your token distribution (40–80 tokens mostly).
- Day 1–2: scale concurrency to pilot target (250 concurrent) and sweep batch sizes / quantization settings to match TTFT SLO.
- Day 3: end-to-end run from your frontend using SSE integration to validate chunk cadence and client render.

If that sounds good I’ll start scheduling the perf runs for next week.

—Rishi
